name: Honolulu
info: Honolulu is a city on the southeast coast of the island of Oʻahu in the Hawaiian archipelago, settled by Polynesian migrants by the 11th century, a harbour town of the nineteenth century and the capital of Hawaii since 1845.

facts.founded: Oral histories and artifacts indicate a settlement where Honolulu now stands in the 11th century, made by the original Polynesian migrants to the archipelago; the city grew from a handful of homes in the early 19th century.
facts.where: On the southeast coast of the island of Oʻahu, in the Pacific Ocean, beside Honolulu Harbor, in the state of Hawaii, United States.
facts.known: Honolulu Harbor; the capital of the Hawaiian Kingdom from 1845; ʻIolani Palace; the overthrow of the monarchy in 1893 and annexation by the United States in 1898; the fire of 1900; the attack on Pearl Harbor in 1941; statehood in 1959
facts.today: Honolulu is the capital and most populous city of the state of Hawaii and the county seat of the consolidated City and County of Honolulu.

sections.origins:
Honolulu lies on the southeast coast of the island of Oʻahu. Its name is Hawaiian for sheltered harbor or calm port, and the harbour and the geography of the area have long made it desirable as a port. The older name of the district, Kou, roughly covered the area from Nuʻuanu Avenue to Alakea Street and from Hotel Street to Queen Street, which is the heart of the present downtown. Oral histories and artifacts indicate that the original Polynesian migrants to the archipelago had a settlement where Honolulu now stands in the 11th century.

The land behind the harbour is volcanic. The volcanic field of the Honolulu Volcanics lies partly inside the city, Diamond Head stands beside Waikiki, and the districts of Salt Lake and Āliamanu are built in extinct tuff cones. Punchbowl Crater fronts Pauoa Valley. Honolulu has a hot semi-arid climate because of a rain shadow, with an annual average rainfall of 16.41 inches (417 millimetres), most of it from October through early April. The city is also remote: the nearest point of the mainland United States, in northern California, is 2,045 nautical miles away.
sections.growth:
The settlement grew from a handful of homes to a city in the early 19th century. After Kamehameha I chose it in 1810 as a replacement for his residence at Waikiki, foreign ships increasingly called at the harbour, and the port became a focal point for merchant ships travelling between North America and Asia. The first foreigner to sail in, Captain William Brown of Great Britain, had arrived in November 1794.

Honolulu became the islands' centre of commerce once it was the capital, and descendants of American missionaries established major businesses downtown. The kings who followed Kamehameha III transformed it into a modern capital and put up buildings such as St. Andrew's Cathedral, ʻIolani Palace and Aliʻiōlani Hale. Electric street railways added to the city's equipment: Hawaiian Tramways began in 1888 and the Honolulu Rapid Transit and Land Company in 1903, and the Honolulu Rapid Transit Company that followed ran until the Second World War.

The Honolulu Symphony was established in 1900. Despite the disasters of the late 19th and early 20th centuries, Honolulu remained the capital, largest city, main airport and seaport of the islands. After statehood an economic boom brought rapid growth to the city and to Hawaii.
sections.rulers:
After Kamehameha I conquered Oʻahu in the Battle of Nuʻuanu at Nuʻuanu Pali, he moved his royal court from the island of Hawaiʻi to Waikiki in 1804. In 1809 the court relocated to what is now downtown Honolulu, and in 1812 the capital was moved back to Kailua-Kona. The choice of Honolulu in place of his residence at Waikiki is also dated 1810, so the order of these moves is not fully settled.

He and the kings who followed him made Honolulu a modern capital. In 1845 Kamehameha III moved the permanent capital of the Hawaiian Kingdom from Lahaina on Maui to Honolulu. Honolulu was then the seat of the independent kingdom until its overthrow in 1893. Hawaii was annexed by the United States in 1898, and the city became the capital of the territory established after annexation. Since 1959 it has been the capital of the state of Hawaii.

Its local government is the consolidated City and County of Honolulu, of which Honolulu is the county seat. The municipal offices, including Honolulu Hale, lie in the Capitol District, which is also the historic centre of the state government and holds the State Capitol, ʻIolani Palace and the statue of King Kamehameha I.
sections.life:
The city's neighbourhoods reflect its uses. Downtown is the financial, commercial and governmental centre, and Aloha Tower stands on the waterfront. The Chinatown Historic District includes the former Hotel Street Vice District. Kakaʻako is a light-industrial district between downtown and Waikiki, and Kalihi and Pālama are working-class neighbourhoods. Mānoa, Mōʻiliʻili and Makiki are residential districts inland, and the main campus of the University of Hawaiʻi is in Mānoa Valley.

The population has been mixed in origin. In 1970 the Census Bureau reported that 33.9% of Honolulu's people were white and 53.7% Asian and Pacific Islander. In the census of 2020, 54.8% of the city's residents were Asian, 17.9% European, 8.4% Native Hawaiian and Other Pacific Islander and 16.3% of two or more races. The largest Asian groups were Japanese (19.9%), Filipino (13.2%) and Chinese (10.4%), and people solely of Native Hawaiian ancestry were 3.2%.

Honolulu also became a place of collections and learning. The Bishop Museum holds the world's largest collection of Hawaiiana and Pacific culture artifacts, and the Honolulu Museum of Art holds the state's largest collection of Asian and Western art. The East–West Center, established by Congress in 1960, is headquartered in Mānoa.
sections.crises:
Four turbulent events fell in the late 19th and early 20th centuries: the overthrow of the Hawaiian monarchy in 1893, annexation by the United States in 1898, a large fire in 1900 and the Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor in 1941. Despite them Honolulu remained the capital, the largest city and the main seaport of the Hawaiian Islands.

On 17 January 1893 the Committee of Safety, seven foreign-born permanent residents and six Hawaiian-born people, deposed Queen Liliʻuokalani. Henry E. Cooper, its chairman, read a proclamation before ʻIolani Palace that set up a Provisional Government under Sanford B. Dole, and the American minister John L. Stevens landed 162 sailors and Marines. The queen yielded under protest to the superior force of the United States, to avoid a collision of armed forces and perhaps loss of life. President Cleveland's investigator, James Blount, held American representatives responsible. The Republic of Hawaii was declared in 1894 and annexation came in 1898, when most of the 40,000 Native Hawaiians protested by staying in their homes. Congress apologised in 1993.

On 7 December 1941 the Empire of Japan attacked Pearl Harbor, which lies just outside the city, and the attack prompted the entry of the United States into the Second World War. The attack gave the city worldwide recognition, and the harbour remains a major base of the United States Navy and home of the United States Pacific Fleet.

Hurricanes are rare in Honolulu; the last recorded one to hit near the city was the Category 4 Hurricane Iniki in 1992. Since the beginning of the 21st century drought, water shortages and sea level rise have affected the city, with flooding of beaches and hotels in downtown Honolulu.
sections.legacy:
Honolulu holds the buildings of the monarchy. ʻIolani Palace, Aliʻiōlani Hale and St. Andrew's Cathedral were raised by the kings of the nineteenth century, and the statue of Kamehameha I stands in the Capitol District. The Bishop Museum keeps the largest collection of Hawaiian and Pacific artifacts in the world.

The city is today the capital and most populous city of the state of Hawaii and the county seat of the City and County of Honolulu, which covers its part of the southeast coast of Oʻahu. The Urban Honolulu census area has an area of 68.4 square miles (177.2 square kilometres), and the population was 350,964 at the census of 2020, up from 337,256 in 2010. The metropolitan area, which takes in all of Oʻahu, had 1,016,508 people in 2020.

The harbour that gave Honolulu its name is still its port, and the harbour at Pearl Harbor nearby remains a major base of the United States Navy. The city's mix of Asian, Western and Pacific peoples shows in its population, and the National Memorial Cemetery of the Pacific lies in Punchbowl Crater. Waikiki, once the residence of Kamehameha I, is now a district of the city.

summary: Honolulu, on the southeast coast of Oʻahu, was a Polynesian settlement by the 11th century and grew around its harbour in the early 19th. It became the capital of the Hawaiian Kingdom in 1845 and of the territory and state of Hawaii after the overthrow of 1893 and annexation in 1898.
